p056.title: A real friend
sentences: Julia is 11.
She has got curly, brown hair, brown eyes and a big smile.
She's got a lot of friends at school.
All her classmates like her.
At lunchtime, Julia always goes to the school canteen and buys her lunch.
Her friend, Jack, doesn't buy any food.
He just drinks a glass of water.
Jack does this every day, and Julia is worried.
One day, she asks Jack, 'Are you hungry?'
'Yes,' says Jack.
'But you don't eat at school,' says Julia.
'I haven't got any money for lunch,' says Jack.
'My dad hasn't got a job and my mum's ill.
They've got lots of problems.
But don't worry about me – I'm OK.'
Julia thinks about this.
At home, she's got a big glass jar.
It's full of coins.
She wants to buy an electric scooter one day.
That night, Julia opens the jar, takes the coins and puts them into a bag.
Her mum sees her.
'Why are you doing that?' she asks.
'My friend Jack hasn't got any lunch money and I've got some money here.
This is for him.'
'That's very kind of you,' says her mum.
She feels happy that her daughter wants to do this.
The next day, Julia and her mum go and see her teacher.
They tell her about Jack and Julia gives her the money.
'This is for Jack's lunch.
Now, he can have lunch every day,' she says.
Julia hasn't got an electric scooter, but she's got a happy friend – Jack!

p059.title: A present for Annie
sentences: Hello, can I help?
Yes. Have you got anything I can give to my best friend? It's a present.
Yes, we've got a lot of things. Is it for a girl or a boy?
It's for a girl, for my friend, Annie.
OK. I've got this lovely little yellow rose. Yellow's a happy colour. It's a lovely present for a girl. It's got a necklace with it.
Have you got any little animals?
Yes, we've got a little silver dolphin or a dog. They both show friendship.
Oh, I love the dolphin, and Annie likes dolphins, too. They're her favourite animal. But she's got a dog. It's just like this one.
Hmm. So maybe the dog or the dolphin. I've got one more to show you. It's really beautiful.
Oh, it's a heart. And it's in two pieces. That's clever.
Yes. You wear one piece and your friend, Annie, wears the other.
Oh, that's so cool. I like that idea, but I still prefer the dolphin. How much is it?
That's OK. Can I have the dolphin, then?
Of course. And do you want the necklace too?
No. Annie's got a nice silver necklace. She doesn't need another one.
OK, then. That's £15. I've got a little bag you can put it in.
Oh, that's great. Thank you.
I hope she likes it.

p060.title: The new teacher
sentences: Hi, Oliver. Good to see you.
Hi, Ellie. You look happy. How's it going? How's your first day back at school?
Not too bad, thanks. We've got this great new teacher. You'd really like him.
Really? Lucky you. What does he teach?
Science.
But you don't like Science.
I do now. This new teacher's very funny. He makes us all laugh and he makes Science fun. And I understand everything. It's great.
Really? What does this new teacher look like?
Well, he's quite tall and he's slim. He's got brown eyes and he wears glasses. He's got short curly hair. It's red like yours.
He's got red hair?
Yes, like yours but your hair is straight and his is curly.
Has he got a beard?
Yes, he's got a short beard.
And has he got a moustache?
Yes … Oh, and he likes sport. He plays rugby and he likes football. He goes to football matches at the weekends with his son. His son's the same age as us.
Really? And his favourite team is Manchester City.
Yes, it is. How do you know?
Is this him walking towards us now?
Yes, it is.
That's my dad.
No way! You're kidding!

p063.title: Welcoming people around the world
sentences: How do you say hello to someone you know?
Do you smile? Do you touch the other person?
Here are some ideas for travellers.
This is how people in different countries welcome each other.
Do you do different things in your country?
In many countries in Asia, people bow their heads when they meet each other.
This shows respect.
In India, Nepal and Bangladesh, people bring their hands together in front of their heart and say 'Namaste'.
When you greet a grandmother or grandfather or another older person in Turkey, you kiss their right hand and then place it on your forehead.
They do this in the Philippines, too.
The Maori people in New Zealand rub noses together when they meet.
This is called the 'hongi'.
In Malaysia, you put your hand on your heart and nod your head.
Sometimes you also take the person's hands in your hands first.
In Western countries, many people shake hands when they meet.
Sometimes they just smile and say something like 'Hello!' or 'Hi!'
In the US and in other countries, some people like using a 'fist bump' to greet another person.
Both people make a fist, push their arm forward slowly and touch each other's fists.
In many countries around the world, friends kiss each other on the cheek.
In some countries they kiss one cheek, in others they kiss both cheeks and in some they kiss cheeks three times.
